justification_text:
When I made these probabilistic forecasts, the point estimates at each horizon were primarily informed by recent trends, historical patterns, and any data suggesting how the variable in question was behaving in the short, medium, and longer-term. For the 1-day horizon, the point estimate of 24.32 reflects the strongest anchoring to the most recent observed value or predictive factors, as very short-term changes are typically more predictable and tend to exhibit less variance. By the 1-week mark, the point estimate shifts slightly to 24.3, reflecting the possibility of small disturbances or adjustments beyond daily fluctuations. For the 1-month horizon, the point estimate of 24.2 begins to take into account the possibility of more substantial adjustments over time, whether due to emerging trends or longer-term reversion toward a baseline.

The widths of the confidence intervals were influenced by increasing uncertainty as the forecast horizons lengthen. In the 1-day projections, uncertainty remains tight (90% CI: [24.0, 24.64]) because the time frame is so short that unexpected shocks or unusual events are less likely to diverge dramatically from the estimate. By the 1-week horizon, the uncertainty naturally widens (90% CI: [23.5, 25.1]) due to the potential for more cumulative deviations, whether caused by internal variability in the system being modeled or external influencing factors. At the 1-month horizon, the confidence interval becomes even broader (90% CI: [22.5, 25.9]), as longer timescales introduce the possibility of larger, less predictable influences or systemic shifts that aren’t apparent in shorter-term observations.

Specific risks or events could push future outcomes outside these intervals. For instance, if there are external shocks like unexpected policy changes, major global news events, or disruptive market conditions, such events could significantly alter the trajectory of the forecast. These types of shocks are hard to model explicitly, but their potential impact grows with time, which explains why the longer-term intervals are wider. Additionally, structural breaks—such as an unprecedented change in the underlying dynamics of the system I'm forecasting—could invalidate the assumptions used to predict future values altogether, creating outcomes far outside the stated intervals. Such risks tend to be rare but are always worth considering as a possibility.
